name: Ultraviolet Cone Cell Expansion
description: Introduces a fourth cone cell type sensitive to near-ultraviolet light (300–400nm), modeled on the tetrachromatic vision of mantis shrimp and birds. The user perceives an entirely new range of color invisible to unmodified humans. UV-reflective materials, biological fluids, certain inks, and structural coloration all become visible. The world looks fundamentally different — flowers have guide-patterns, fabrics reveal hidden dyes, and human skin shows sun damage, vein patterns, and applied chemicals with startling clarity. Forensic investigators, art authenticators, and security professionals value the modification highly. The subjective experience of seeing a new primary color is reportedly disorienting for the first few weeks — the brain has no existing framework for processing ultraviolet, and users describe the new color as 'painful blue' or 'electric nothing' until their visual cortex adapts.
source_organism: Odontodactylus scyllarus (mantis shrimp), synthetic photoreceptor proteins
legality: Licensed (requires registration due to forensic applications)
procedure: Retinal injection with photoreceptor growth factor, 2 sessions
side_effects: Headaches during neural adaptation as brain learns to process new color
Difficulty sleeping — UV component of artificial lighting becomes visible and irritating
Social discomfort from seeing biological details on other people's skin
Rare: synesthetic cross-wiring with other senses during adaptation
social_perception: Professional-class modification. Respected but sometimes unsettling — UV users see things about you that you can't see about yourself. Some people find it invasive. UV-blocking cosmetics are sold specifically to defeat UV vision.
story_hooks: A UV-vision user discovers that a common cosmetic product fluoresces in a pattern that spells out a corporate logo — a hidden branding campaign written in light humans can't normally see
An investigator's UV vision reveals that a 'natural death' scene is covered in biological traces that tell a very different story
